At the end of eight hours diffillation, I drew off one-fourth of the contents of the veffel; a fecond fourth two hours afterwards; a third fourth after ten hours and a half, or eleven hours ; and the reft after twelve hours diftillation, which formed the conclusion. " When the liquor is entirely drawn off from the veffel, it must again be immediately filled with water, or at least to the height of five or fix inches above the return of the leaden tube, otherwise the gas, which continues to escape from the difilling veffel and then affords no refillance, might attack the pneumatic veffel itself. 250. " The fire muft be taken from beneath the retort as foon as the diftillation is finished, not only to prevent the effect of the gafcous vapours, which fill continue flowly to escape, from acting on the fides of the tub, but likewise to diffuse the retorts or bodies to receive a quantity of warm water, which is to be poured in up to the neck. There is no realon to fear an excess of quantity, and the hotter the veffels are the better. It is effential, however, that it be not poured in cold, for fear of breaking the glafs. The adopter is then to be unluted from the neck of the leaden tube, if the operator choofes ; and in order that no vapour may escape into the workhop, a bit of lute or a cork may be applied to the beak of the adopter. The land bath easily permits the retort to be raifed and returned again to its place, as well as the application of the lute or flopper to the neck of the adopter, this latt being raifed with one hand while the cork is put in with the other. " Neverthelefs, as the lutes which connect the adopter with the retort are fomewhat footened towards the end of the operation, it would be more prudent to leave every thing in its place, for fear of deranging those lutes. This danger is greater when the adopter is of lead, because the great length of this additional piece tends to force the luting fill more on that account. Wikipedia article "Textile bleaching", passages:
<wikipedia>
[1] Bleaching can be dated back to at least 1000 BC from an Egyptian list found in the tomb of Rekh-mi-re at Thebes, which mentioned both bleached and unbleached linen. Mulrooney dates it back as far as 5000 BC, while Walton claims it was introduced to Egypt from Asia. It’s plausible that it was discovered independently by different cultures. It’s generally assumed to have developed after noticing that garments are naturally bleached by sunlight and washing. Wood ash (potash, or impure potassium hydroxide) was an early form of soap, known to have been used in bleaching since at least 1 AD. This process of washing cloth in a solution of ashes (lye) and left in the sun, known as Grassing, is one of the oldest methods of bleaching textile goods. To bleach linen and cotton -based fabrics, the Grassing method has been used. Linen has long been bleached in Europe with Grassing method. The linens were laid out on the grass for over seven days after boiling with the ''lyes of ashes and rinsing''. Bleachfield was an open area to spread cloth, it was a field near watercourse used by a bleachery. Bleachfields were common in and around the mill towns during the British Industrial Revolution

[2] The Dutch were bleaching by about the 12th century and are credited with soaking the bleached cloth in a bath of soured milk for 5–8 days. This softened and neutralised the harsh effects of the caustic lye. By the 17th century the Dutch were renowned for their bleaching skills and much of their trade was for customers abroad. Around 1756 an alternative to soured milk was proposed by the Scottish doctor, Francis Home using a weak solution of sulphuric acid. This was made commercially viable by John Roebuck's manufacture of sulphuric acid and reduced the soaking time to 12–24 hours. A final rinse and drying finished the bleaching process. The English East India Company imported bleached, painted and printed calico from India during the 17th century. This disrupted the English silk and wool trades and an act of parliament, the Encouragement of Manufactures Act 1698 (11 Will. 3. c. 10), was passed that prohibited the wearing of printed calicos manufactured in China, India or Persia. This inadvertently established a calico bleaching and printing industry using unbleached Indian calico.

[3] The term "bleach" originates from a French word signifying "to whiten". In essence, the process of bleaching involves whitening by removing substances that impart color to the material undergoing the bleaching treatment. Bleaching is the process of decolorizing the material after it has been scoured.: 169 Bleaching textiles can be classified as oxidative bleaching and reductive bleaching which can be carried out with oxidizing and reductive bleaching agents.: 161 Bleaching agents attack the chromophores and alter the color absorbing properties of the objects. Generally oxidative bleachings are carried out using sodium hypochlorite, sodium chlorite or sulfuric acid. Vegetable fibres, animal fibers, and mineral fibres are the three major types of natural fibers. Natural fibers such as cotton, ramie, jute, wool, and regenerated fibers such as bamboo are all generally bleached with oxidative methods. It is the conjugated double bonds of the substrate that makes the substrate capable of absorbing visible light. Hence, it looks yellower and need bleaching. When bleaching action carries out with oxygen, it removes the chromophoric sites and makes the cloths whiter.
</wikipedia>
